title: Dimensional Modeling Basics
summary: Facts, dimensions, and grain are the vocabulary every analytics schema is built from. Get grain wrong and every downstream query is a little bit lying to you.

slides.markdown:
Analytics modeling has its own vocabulary, and almost everything else in this group builds on two words: **facts** and **dimensions**.

A **fact** is something that happened — an order, a page view, a payment — with numbers attached. A **dimension** is the descriptive context around it — which customer, which product, which day. Split those apart deliberately, and you can slice any fact by any dimension without redesigning anything.

The single decision that determines whether this works is **grain**: exactly what one row of the fact table represents. Get grain wrong and no amount of clever SQL fixes the numbers downstream.

slides.subTitle: What happened vs who/what/when it happened to
slides.markdown:
A **fact table** holds measurements of events: `order_total`, `quantity`, `latency_ms`. Every column is either a number you'll aggregate or a foreign key pointing at a dimension.

A **dimension table** holds the descriptive attributes you filter and group by: customer name, product category, store region, calendar date. Dimensions answer "who, what, where, when" — facts answer "how much, how many."

The split is deliberate: it lets you ask "total revenue by region, by month, by product category" as a single join-and-aggregate query, instead of writing bespoke SQL for every combination someone might ask about. Almost every analytics question is really "aggregate some fact, sliced by some combination of dimensions."

slides.sectionTitle: Grain: the decision everything else depends on
slides.markdown:
**Grain** is a one-sentence declaration of what a single fact row represents: "one row per line item per order," or "one row per session per day." You choose it before you design a single column.

Grain has to be exact, not approximate. "One row per order" and "one row per order line item" sound similar but produce completely different tables — the second has a `product_id` and `quantity` that the first can't have, because an order can contain many products.

Every measure, every dimension key, and every question you can answer later is a consequence of this one sentence. Declare it explicitly and write it in the table's documentation — "the grain of `fct_orders` is one row per order" — so nobody has to reverse-engineer it from the data six months later.

slides.sectionTitle: A fact table surrounded by its dimensions
slides.markdown:
The classic shape: one fact table in the middle, with a foreign key out to each dimension that describes it. This is where the name **star schema** comes from — draw the joins and it looks like a star.

A sales fact typically points at a product dimension, a customer dimension, a store dimension, and a date dimension — four foreign keys, plus the numeric measures like `quantity` and `revenue`.

slides.subTitle: The deliberate opposite of OLTP design
slides.markdown:
A transactional (OLTP) schema is [normalized](normalization) to avoid duplicate data and keep writes consistent — a customer's city lives in exactly one row, referenced everywhere by key. That's the right call when the workload is thousands of small writes a second.

Analytics workloads are the opposite: a handful of huge reads, almost no writes. Dimension tables deliberately **denormalize** — a product dimension might repeat "Electronics" as a category name on ten thousand rows instead of normalizing it into a separate category table.

The payoff is fewer joins per query and much simpler SQL for whoever's writing the report. The cost — some duplicated text, more storage — is cheap on a columnar warehouse that compresses repeated values almost for free. Optimizing for read simplicity over write efficiency is the whole point of dimensional modeling.

slides.sectionTitle: Mixing two grains in one fact table
slides.markdown:
The most common way a fact table breaks: someone appends order-level summary rows into a table whose grain is order **line items**.

Now `SUM(revenue)` double-counts every order that has both a summary row and its line-item rows. Nothing in the schema stops this — the table happily accepts both kinds of rows, and the bug only surfaces when someone's total looks roughly 2x too high and nobody can figure out why.

The fix is structural, not a query patch: one fact table, one grain, always. If you need order-level totals *and* line-item detail, that's two fact tables — `fct_orders` and `fct_order_lines` — not one table wearing two hats. A grain violation is a schema bug, not a data-quality bug, so no downstream validation catches it reliably; the only real defense is declaring and enforcing grain at design time.

slides.subTitle: One customer, one date, shared everywhere
slides.markdown:
A **conformed dimension** is a single dimension table — same keys, same attributes, same meaning — reused across multiple fact tables. One `dim_date`, one `dim_customer`, referenced by `fct_orders`, `fct_support_tickets`, and `fct_marketing_emails` alike.

Without conformance, each team builds its own "customer" table with slightly different definitions of active, churned, or enterprise — and now a revenue report and a support report disagree about basic facts like customer count, for no real reason.

Conformed dimensions are what let you join across fact tables at all: "revenue per support ticket" only makes sense if both facts key into the *same* customer and date dimensions. This is also the seed of the semantic-layer idea covered later in this group — shared definitions, enforced once, not reinvented per report.

Two small patterns that come up constantly once you start building real fact tables:

- A **degenerate dimension** is a dimension-like value that lives directly on the fact table with no dimension table behind it, because it has no real attributes of its own — an `order_number` or invoice number, kept for grouping and drill-through, not for filtering by a description.
- A **junk dimension** bundles a handful of low-cardinality flags — `is_gift`, `payment_method`, `promo_applied` — into one small dimension table, instead of littering the fact table with a dozen tiny foreign keys or leaving them as raw flags with no shared home.

Both exist for the same reason: not every attribute deserves its own dimension table, and forcing one onto everything just adds joins without adding value.

slides.sectionTitle: Why this shape wins on a columnar warehouse
slides.subTitle: The numbers behind the design
slides.markdown:
Modern columnar warehouses (BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift) make the star schema's trade-offs even more one-sided in its favor.

A repeated string like a category name compresses to a handful of bytes per row under dictionary encoding, so the "wasted" duplication in a denormalized dimension is close to free — often under 1% of a fact table's storage footprint. Meanwhile a join in a columnar engine scans and hashes full columns, and every extra join adds a network shuffle in a distributed warehouse.

So the real cost comparison isn't "a bit more storage" vs "no extra joins" — it's *cheap, compressible storage* vs *joins that get more expensive as fact tables grow into billions of rows*. That asymmetry is why star schema, not snowflake or fully normalized OLTP-style modeling, is the default for warehouse analytics.

A junior modeler starts with the columns available and figures out the grain afterward, by looking at what the data seems to support. A senior modeler states the grain **first**, as a sentence, before touching a column list — then designs the table to guarantee it.

That ordering matters because grain constrains everything downstream: which measures are even valid (a later topic in this group covers additive vs semi-additive measures), which joins are safe, and whether a `COUNT(*)` means anything. Ask a candidate to design a fact table and watch whether grain is the first sentence out of their mouth or something they back into after three follow-up questions — it's one of the fastest signals of real dimensional-modeling experience.
